title: Estimation of Engineering Properties for Coconut Shell Powder Reinforced 100% Bio-Degradable Beeswax Composites to Replace Wood Materials
author: B T, G V, et al.

steps.title: Extract raw beeswax from honeycombs
steps.instruction: Remove honey from combs, wash thoroughly, cut combs into small pieces, place in a pan, add clean water to fully cover, heat gently while stirring continuously until the combs melt completely.

substeps.instruction: Remove honey and wash combs thoroughly.
Cut cleaned combs into small pieces.
Place pieces in a pan and add enough clean water to cover them.
Heat the mixture gently, stirring continuously to avoid ignition, until the combs are fully melted.

steps.title: Separate wax from water and debris
steps.instruction: Pour the molten mixture into a tightly sealed heavy‑fabric bag, squeeze the bag over a basin using two wooden blocks to extract wax, let the water‑wax mixture cool, then collect the solid wax disc formed on the water surface and scrape off any residual material.

substeps.instruction: Transfer the hot mixture into a long, tightly secured bag made of heavy fabric (e.g., sacking, woven rush, nylon, jute).
Place the bag over a basin or bucket and squeeze it with two pieces of wood to extract the wax, leaving larger debris behind.
Allow the bucket with hot water and molten wax to cool in a clean, sheltered location.
When cooled, a wax disc will form on the water surface; remove this disc.
Scrape off any residual material on the underside of the wax disc.

steps.title: Purify wax via water re‑melting
steps.instruction: Re‑melt the collected wax with an equal volume of clean water, strain through fine cotton cloth into a lightly soaped enamel bowl (max 2 kg wax, using non‑fat, unscented soap), cool for ~12 h in a dust‑free area, then remove the solid wax and scrape bottom impurities with a sharp knife.

substeps.instruction: Re‑melt the wax together with an equal volume of clean water.
Strain the hot mixture through a finer cotton cloth.
Collect the filtrate in a lightly soaped enamel bowl that can hold no more than two kilograms of wax; avoid fat‑containing or heavily scented soap.
Allow the mixture to cool for approximately 12 hours in a dust‑ and wind‑free area.
After cooling, remove the solid wax from the bowl.
Scrape any impurities adhering to the bottom of the wax with a sharp knife.

steps.title: Prepare coconut shell powder fractions
steps.instruction: Mechanically mill raw coconut shell material, then vibratory‑sieve the milled powder to obtain five size fractions: 425 µm, 300 µm, 212 µm, 150 µm, and 106 µm, following ISO 3310‑1:2016 and ASTM E11‑23 guidelines.

substeps.instruction: Mechanically mill the raw coconut shell material (e.g., ball or roller mill) to fracture particles.
Pass the milled powder through a vibratory sieve stack equipped with standard sieves matching the target sizes.
Collect the fraction retained between each pair of sieves to obtain the five size ranges: 425 µm, 300 µm, 212 µm, 150 µm, and 106 µm.
Iteratively mill and sieve as needed to achieve narrow size distributions per ISO 3310‑1:2016 and ASTM E11‑23.

steps.title: Combine wax, powder, and xanthan gum
steps.instruction: Weigh the desired amounts of purified beeswax and a selected CNS powder fraction, place them in a hot pan, add 1 %–2 % (w/w) xanthan gum, and mix thoroughly until a homogeneous mass is obtained.

substeps.instruction: Measure the required weight of beeswax.
Measure the required weight of the chosen CNS powder fraction (425, 300, 212, 150, or 106 µm).
Add 1 % to 2 % (by weight) xanthan gum to the mixture.
Heat the pan and mix the components thoroughly to obtain a uniform blend.

steps.title: High‑shear mix and add stabilizers
steps.instruction: Subject the wax‑powder‑xanthan mixture to high‑shear mixing at 70 °C for 4 min at 12 000 rpm, then add glycerol and cellulose nanofibers to increase viscosity and maintain dispersion stability.

substeps.instruction: Set the mixer to 70 °C.
Mix at 12 000 rpm for 4 minutes.
Add glycerol (quantity as required for viscosity) and cellulose nanofibers (quantity as required for stability).
Continue mixing briefly to ensure uniform distribution of the stabilizers.

steps.title: Mold mixture and cure
steps.instruction: Transfer the homogeneous composite mixture into a mould, allow it to cool and solidify for 24 hours at ambient conditions.

substeps.instruction: Pour the hot mixture into the desired mould.
Leave the mould undisturbed for 24 hours to permit cooling and complete solidification.

steps.title: Machine test specimens to ASTM dimensions
steps.instruction: Cut cured composite blocks into tensile specimens of 200 × 20 × 5 mm (L × B × T) per ASTM‑D3039‑M08 and flexural specimens of 120 × 12 × 5 mm per ASTM‑790‑M.

substeps.instruction: Using a precision saw, cut specimens for tensile testing to 200 mm length, 20 mm width, 5 mm thickness.
Cut specimens for flexural testing to 120 mm length, 12 mm width, 5 mm thickness.

steps.title: Determine sample density by Archimedes
steps.instruction: Measure the density of each specimen using the Archimedes (buoyancy) method as described in ASTM D792, then compare measured values with theoretical rule‑of‑mixtures densities.

substeps.instruction: Weigh each specimen in air.
Submerge the specimen in water and record the apparent weight.
Calculate density using the Archimedes principle per ASTM D792.
Compare the experimental density with theoretical values obtained from the rule of mixtures.

description: In Bio composites are materials composed of natural fibers or particles, such as bamboo, hemp, flax or coconut, embedded in a polymer matrix. They offer a sustainable alternative to traditional composites, reducing reliance on non-renewable resources and lowering environmental impact. Bio composites are valued for their lightweight nature, biodegradability, and often comparable mechanical properties to synthetic composites, making them attractive for a range of applications from automotive and construction to consumer goods and packaging. In recent years, there has been a growing demand for biodegradable composites reinforced with natural fillers sourced from plant fibers [14]. Fibers such as jute, flax, hemp, banana, sisal, and coconut provide excellent alternatives to synthetic fibers, reducing dependence on non-renewable resources and decreasing pollution and greenhouse gas emissions [15]. These natural fiber fillers offer several benefits, including low cost, high toughness, corrosion resistance, low density, good specific strength properties, reduced tool wear, and biodegradability. Wood is prominent because of its remarkable heat resistance and non-melting properties. Wood, primarily composed of cellulose, lignin, and water, each with specific melting points, transforms under heat, producing various substances such as charcoal, methanol, and carbon dioxide. Lignin can be considered an effective environmentally friendly alternative to BPA, acting as a source of phenolic compounds. The content of these compounds is not readily predictable across various extraction processes, as indicated in the review by Lu and Gu [16]. Lignin is highly accessible and is the second most abundant organic material on Earth, following cellulose. It can be extracted from multiple sources, including wood, cotton, jute, hemp, and black liquor.
